build_plan.exit_criteria: All four panels build, fit a 200 mm bed, pass the 0.80 mm wall and 45 degree overhang gates, and every terrain pocket is a blind 6.00 mm hole with 1.00 mm of panel wall wherever it reaches a seam.

Belt and corona tiles build, drop into the same pocket at 0.25 mm per side where that pocket's edge lands on a panel seam and 0.65 mm in an open pocket, and present no raised feature under a seated disc: measured on the belt tile, nothing reaches above the field datum and a seated disc rests on 532.9 mm2 of coplanar contact.
Both stars build with a flat top face, a drafted flange skirt and two flames that print without support.
Both trays build with eight identical sockets that take a Ø34.00 disc at 0.20 mm per side.
Both disc profiles build with opposite draft directions and carry a flush numeral inlay that leaves the printed wall smooth.
Eight globes build on the measured ladder, strictly increasing from 16.78 to 29.97 mm of total piece height, each meeting its seat at latitude -42 degrees.
Every inner-planet marking builds as a flush inlay that partitions its globe exactly, with no material lost and no overlap between markings.
Every outer-planet marking builds as a flush inlay, and Saturn's ring carries a web that holds its underside steeper than the 45 degree overhang gate.

components.duty: Carries one quarter of the 7 by 9 field at a 36.00 mm cell pitch and holds files a to c, ranks 1 to 4; trap c1 and belt cells b4 and c4.
components.form: A flat dark_gray slab 9.00 mm thick. The playing grid is cut into its face as a 1.20 mm wide, 0.60 mm deep square-bottomed groove on each boundary between two land cells, so a piece stands on the board instead of sinking into it. Terrain is the only depth: each den, trap and belt cell is a blind 6.00 mm pocket, 34.80 mm across in the open and 34.40 mm across where an edge lands on a panel seam.
components.interfaces: Butt seam to the neighbouring panels, 1.00 mm of panel wall beside any pocket that reaches a seam; blind pockets take the belt tiles, corona tiles and den spigots at 0.25 mm of slip per side where the pocket edge lands on a panel seam and 0.65 mm in an open pocket.
components.name: Board panel southwest
components.placement: Butts against its neighbouring panels along the seam after file c and the seam after rank 4; together the four panels make a 268 by 340 mm board with an 8.00 mm border.

components.duty: Shows the water as an asteroid belt without enforcing it: any world will stand level on the pad, because the belt is a picture of an exclusion rather than an enforcement of one. Twelve identical tiles fill the twelve belt cells.
components.form: A 33.50 mm square cocoa_brown tile 6.00 mm thick, four-fold symmetric about its own centre. Its floor sits 2.00 mm below the field datum and carries forty-eight faceted boulders of radius 1.60 to 2.60 mm. No rock touches another and none ends in a point: every one is a flat-topped frustum held 0.35 mm clear of tangency with its neighbours, with the landing pad and with the tile's own edge. At the centre is a smooth Ø26.00 landing pad flush with the field.
components.interfaces: 0.25 mm of slip per side where the pocket edge lands on a panel seam and 0.65 mm in an open pocket; top face coplanar with the field datum so the cut grid reads unbroken straight through the water. Measured on the exact solid: nothing on the tile reaches above the field datum, and a seated disc rests on 532.9 mm² of coplanar contact — the Ø26.00 pad plus four crests in its plane — so it cannot rock.
components.name: Asteroid belt tile
components.placement: Drops into a belt pocket on files b, c, e and f at ranks 4, 5 and 6, top face flush with the field.

components.duty: Is the den. A world that reaches it has won, and it seats on the star exactly as it seats on any land cell, one step higher. This is the one component in the set allowed to break the legibility floor, and the two flames it carries are what it is paid for.
components.form: A 36.00 mm square sunflower_yellow flange standing 2.20 mm proud of the field on a 33.50 mm spigot buried 6.00 mm in the den pocket, the flange drafted off the spigot at 46 degrees from horizontal and finished with a 0.90 mm vertical rim. The top face is flat and clear; hexagonal granulation is engraved 0.40 mm into the four corners a seated disc never covers.
components.interfaces: 0.25 mm of slip per side where the pocket edge lands on a panel seam and 0.65 mm in an open pocket into the den pocket; flat top face at field datum plus 2.20 mm; 0.86 mm of clearance from each flame base to the disc of a world standing on the den; the whole part, flames included, stays inside the 36.00 mm cell footprint.
components.name: Sol star
components.placement: Den cell d1, spigot in the pocket, flange covering the cell, flames at the two corners that face the board border.

components.duty: Makes the near star the focal point of the fixed product frame and the tallest thing on the board. Records its cost in the same breath: from the seat opposite this den the flames stand between the eye and the den cell's far edge.
components.form: Two tapered orange flames rising 18.00 mm above the field from the flange, leaning 12 degrees outward, full at a 6.00 mm foot and drawn out to a 1.50 mm tongue. The two feet sit 20.80 mm apart on the flange diagonal, so each flame stands wholly on solid flange and its outermost lean still falls 17.71 mm from the cell centre, inside the 18.00 mm flange half-width. Nothing is clipped and nothing overhangs the cell.
components.interfaces: Printed as one body with the Sol star in a second filament; every flame face is steeper than 45 degrees from horizontal and rises from the flange, so no part of it is unsupported; the flames never cross the cell boundary, so no neighbouring world can foul them.
components.name: Sol prominences
components.placement: Grows from the Sol star's flange, at the two corners beyond which 8.00 mm of free board border lies.

components.duty: Is the opposing den. Identical geometry at both ends of the board, because feeding your own star is a rule and not a shape.
components.form: The same 36.00 mm square flange and 33.50 mm spigot as the Sol star, printed in black.
components.interfaces: 0.25 mm of slip per side where the pocket edge lands on a panel seam and 0.65 mm in an open pocket into the den pocket; flat top face at field datum plus 2.20 mm.
components.name: Anti-Sol star
components.placement: Den cell d9, turned 180 degrees so its flames face the far border.

components.duty: Marks the far star and balances the frame against the near one.
components.form: Two tapered cyan flames, the mirror of the Sol pair.
components.interfaces: Printed as one body with the Anti-Sol star in a second filament.
components.name: Anti-Sol prominences
components.placement: Grows from the Anti-Sol star's flange at the two border-facing corners.

components.duty: Is the trap. A world standing here has strength 0, and it sits 3.00 mm below the plane inside a ring of the star's own colour, so the reason is visible across the table. Three of these ring each den; the flames are engraved rather than raised because raised relief under a seated disc would make a trapped piece rock.
components.form: A 33.50 mm square orange tile 3.00 mm thick that floors a terrain pocket and leaves a 3.00 mm well above it, the board's own pocket wall making the well. Its face carries an engraved star and sixteen radiating flame tongues cut 0.40 mm deep, and two tapered tongues rise 4.00 mm above the field from the two corners furthest from the den.
components.interfaces: 0.25 mm of slip per side where the pocket edge lands on a panel seam and 0.65 mm in an open pocket into the board pocket; the seated disc drops 3.00 mm and keeps 0.20 mm of slip per side against the pocket wall.
components.name: Sol corona cell
components.placement: Trap cells c1, d2 and e1 around the Sol den and c9, d8 and e9 around the Anti-Sol den, each turned so its tongues point away from its own star.

components.interfaces: 0.20 mm of slip per side for a Ø34.00 disc into a socket.

components.duty: Is the base every world stands on, the constant ruler the eye reads globe diameters against, and one of the three ownership cues: the wall's draft direction and the disc colour both say which army this world belongs to.
components.form: A white disc Ø34.00 by 5.00 mm whose wall flares outward as it rises, drafted 6.5 degrees, top edge rounded 0.60 mm and bottom edge left sharp so the piece sits flat. Its widest measured diameter is Ø33.87.
components.interfaces: Seats flat on a land cell with 1.00 mm to the cell boundary; drops 3.00 mm into a corona well; steps up 2.20 mm onto a star; slips into a tray socket at 0.20 mm per side.
components.name: Sol disc
components.placement: Under every one of the eight worlds on this side of the board.

components.duty: Carries rank on a channel that needs no comparison against a neighbouring piece, and puts it where both seated players read it without touching anything.
components.form: A seven-segment digit 3.60 mm tall, 2.80 mm wide on a 1.00 mm stroke, inlaid flush 0.60 mm into the disc wall in black, repeated at 0 and 180 degrees.
components.interfaces: Flush with the disc wall: the printed part has one smooth outer surface and the colour change is internal.
components.name: Sol rank numeral
components.placement: In the disc wall, centred 2.20 mm above the bed, facing each player.

components.duty: Is rank 1. Its diameter is the fifth root of Mercury's real equatorial diameter against Mercury's, which is what makes the strength ladder a measurement rather than a decision. The seat exists because a sphere resting tangentially on a flat disc leaves an unsupported cap underneath it.
components.form: A gray sphere Ø13.78 mm sunk 2.00 mm into the disc top face and carried by an integral seat cone that springs from latitude -42.0 degrees and spreads outward at 12 degrees from vertical down to the disc. The seat is material added around the globe's foot, finished in the globe's own colour.
components.interfaces: Meets the disc at the seat's Ø10.24 mm landing circle; its surface is a true sphere, so the markings that name the planet are colour inlays and add no relief.
components.name: Mercury globe
components.placement: On the disc of both the Sol and the Anti-Sol Mercury; the globe is a body of revolution and is identical under mirroring.

components.duty: Shows its two-tone albedo map: smooth plains and the Caloris basin, and carries the obliquity: the whole pattern is rotated by Mercury's true axial tilt, toward +X on a Sol world and toward -X on its Anti-Sol mirror.
components.form: A dark_gray colour inlay reaching 1.20 mm into the globe, its outline described in the planet's own frame by latitude, longitude and angular size so that one minimum outline width holds from Mercury to Jupiter.
components.interfaces: Flush with the globe's sphere: the outer surface is unbroken and the colour change is internal, so nothing the marking adds can face downward.
components.name: Mercury plains
components.placement: On the Mercury globe, at its own latitude and longitude in the tilted planet frame.

components.duty: Shows six belts over 60 degrees of latitude, and carries the obliquity: the whole pattern is rotated by Jupiter's true axial tilt, toward +X on a Sol world and toward -X on its Anti-Sol mirror.
components.form: A cocoa_brown colour inlay reaching 1.20 mm into the globe, its outline described in the planet's own frame by latitude, longitude and angular size so that one minimum outline width holds from Mercury to Jupiter.
components.interfaces: Flush with the globe's sphere: the outer surface is unbroken and the colour change is internal, so nothing the marking adds can face downward.
components.name: Jupiter bands
components.placement: On the Jupiter globe, at its own latitude and longitude in the tilted planet frame.

components.duty: Shows the Great Red Spot, and carries the obliquity: the whole pattern is rotated by Jupiter's true axial tilt, toward +X on a Sol world and toward -X on its Anti-Sol mirror.
components.form: A red colour inlay reaching 1.20 mm into the globe, its outline described in the planet's own frame by latitude, longitude and angular size so that one minimum outline width holds from Mercury to Jupiter.
components.interfaces: Flush with the globe's sphere: the outer surface is unbroken and the colour change is internal, so nothing the marking adds can face downward.

concept.interaction: Two players sit across a 7 by 9 field and play Dou Shou Qi exactly as written. Each turn you step one world one square. Rank is the globe's diameter, which is the fifth root of that planet's real equatorial diameter, and it is repeated by a seven-segment numeral inlaid in the disc wall at 0 and 180 degrees. Ownership is the parity inversion of the real axial tilts: a Sol world leans its north pole toward one player and an Anti-Sol world toward the other, the Sol disc flares outward as it rises where the Anti-Sol disc tapers inward, and the discs are white against black. The asteroid belt is twelve cocoa_brown tiles with a flat landing pad at the centre of each, so the water is shown and never enforced. The three trap cells around each den are corona wells: a world standing in one drops 3.00 mm below the field inside a ring in its captor's own colour, and its rank counts for nothing. You win by stepping a world onto the opposing star, a sunflower_yellow plug standing 2.20 mm proud of the field with two flames bursting from the board edge, or by taking every opposing world off the board and into its orbit tray.
concept.summary: Dou Shou Qi, unchanged, played with the eight planets ranked by their real measured diameters. Matter faces antimatter, and you win by walking one of your worlds into the rival sun.
concept.title: Antisol

design_changes.kept: All three rank channels: globe diameter, surface markings, and the numeral at 0 and 180 degrees.
design_changes.what: The rank numeral is a flush colour inlay 0.60 mm into the disc wall, not a 0.45 mm raised relief.
design_changes.why: A 1.00 mm seven-segment stroke standing 0.45 mm proud leaves a down-facing ledge on a wall that drafts away beneath it, and it cannot be chamfered to the 45 degree gate at 2.80 by 3.60 mm without the segments merging. The sealed reference images read the numeral as flush colour.

design_changes.cost: The obliquity lean is a colour cue on seven of the eight planets rather than a silhouette cue. Ownership rests on disc colour, disc draft direction and the lean of the pattern; on Saturn the ring keeps the lean in the silhouette. Total piece heights lose the 1.00 mm of relief, so the ladder runs 16.78 to 29.97 mm and is still strictly increasing.
design_changes.what: Surface markings are flush colour inlays 1.20 mm deep, not 1.00 mm relief with 45 degree chamfered edges.
design_changes.why: A raised patch on the lower half of a sphere presents a rim shallower than the overhang gate allows, and the globe is exposed down to latitude -42 degrees.

design_changes.what: The den plug stands 2.20 mm proud of the field, not 1.00 mm.
design_changes.why: Its flange skirt has to draft off the spigot at more than 45 degrees and still leave a vertical rim thicker than 0.80 mm. At 1.00 mm of proud height the remaining lip measured 0.05 mm over 116 mm2 of surface and failed check_thickness.

design_changes.what: The star's granulation is engraved 0.40 mm into the flange corners, not raised 0.50 mm on the frame.
design_changes.why: A grain half a millimetre tall is thinner than a 0.4 mm nozzle can hold as a wall.

design_changes.what: The corona tile is 33.50 mm square, not 35.50 mm.
design_changes.why: A 35.50 mm tile cannot enter its own 34.80 mm pocket. The tongues moved with it to Ø5.00 on a 20.20 mm diagonal, which keeps 0.70 mm to that cell's own seated disc and 0.37 mm inside the tile edge.

design_changes.what: Sixteen corona tongues starting 6.50 mm from the centre, around an engraved star, not twenty-four running to the middle.
design_changes.why: Run in to the centre the tongues merge into one blob whose boundary leaves 0.13 mm webs over 652 mm2 of surface.

design_changes.what: Saturn's ring is Ø30.00 with a 1.40 mm section, not Ø32.00 by 1.60 mm.
design_changes.why: The Wish's own recorded fallback, taken for the reason the Wish gives: at a 3.00 mm projection the 45 degree web under the ring reads as a funnel rather than as a thickened ring.

design_changes.what: Terrain pockets whose edge lands on a panel seam are inset 1.00 mm instead of 0.60 mm.
design_changes.why: At 0.60 mm each panel carries only half the rib, and check_thickness measured a 0.50 mm wall on all four panels. At 1.00 mm each panel owns a wall it can print and the two panels together part their pockets by 2.00 mm.

design_changes.cost: The flames are slimmer than section 7.2's Ø11.00 and than the reference attempts show, and the printed envelope is 36.00 x 36.00 rather than the 44.10 x 40.10 section 7.2 predicts. The Wish's instruction for the horns risk -- increase the outward lean, do not shorten the flare -- is honoured: the 18.00 mm height and the 12 degree lean are untouched, and the taper is unbroken from foot to tip.
design_changes.what: The prominence feet are Ø6.00 on a 20.80 mm diagonal and stand wholly on the flange, not Ø11.00 on a 23.40 mm diagonal cantilevered outside the cell. Section 7.2's height, count, corners, taper and 12 degree outward lean are all kept.
design_changes.why: Section 7.2 states that the part of each base crossing the cell boundary floats above the field and that nothing needs to be under it. That is not printable, and the gate says so: built exactly as written, check_overhang at 45 degrees reports two unsupported regions of 53.3 mm2 and 51.6 mm2 at the two feet, each with 9.2 mm of air below it and a 10.5 mm span, and returns NEEDS SUPPORT. The measurement is kept at cad/measure/wish-7.2-flare-overhang.md. Cutting the floating part back to a 45 degree roof does print, but it slices a straight face through every flame; a blind critic reading only the renders called it unresolved interpenetration rather than a finished moulding. Ø11.00 cannot both stand on the flange (foot outer edge within the 18.00 mm half-width) and clear the disc of a world seated on the den (foot inner edge beyond 17.44 mm) -- the two conditions are 5.3 mm apart and cannot both hold. Ø6.00 at 20.80 mm satisfies both at once: outermost lean 17.71 mm against 18.00 mm, and 0.86 mm of foot-to-disc clearance.

design_changes.kept: Latitude 22 degrees south for the spot and the inverted pole for Venus's Y, which are the facts; longitude is free.
design_changes.what: Jupiter's Great Red Spot was carried 110 degrees around its own axis and Venus's cloud Y 135 degrees, so that both face the camera. Their latitudes, sizes and colours are untouched.
design_changes.why: Section 8.4 fixes latitudes and names no meridian for either feature, and neither planet carries a prime meridian in this set. On the meridians the first draft used, both features sat on the hidden hemisphere of both armies in every rendered view: measured against the view axis, the spot scored -0.49 and -0.45 and the Y -0.72 and -0.68. A blind reader given only the renders described Jupiter as banded belts with no spot and Venus as a plain white ball, the only one of the eight it could not name. Section 13 requires the opposite of Venus in so many words: its orange cloud Y breaks the outline. After the shift the spot measures +0.44 and +0.62 and the Y +0.63 and +0.81 against the two frames the product is photographed from, on both armies.

design_changes.cost: At 22 degrees the far ranks foreshorten into each other, so the three-position sheet would stop being separable. It is kept at the higher isometric, and the two images therefore do not share a camera.
design_changes.what: The product image is rendered at the Wish's own fixed frame, 35 degrees azimuth and 22 degrees elevation, rather than at a 45/35 isometric. The three-state sheet stays at the isometric.
design_changes.why: Section 13 designs the composition for that camera and says what it buys: at 35/22 the corona wells catch shadow and the tongues catch light, and the cut grid catches light along one wall of every groove. The low elevation is also what puts the globes rather than the board in front of the eye.

design_changes.kept: Every latitude, longitude and angular size the markings were drawn with. One visible consequence is an improvement: Mars's caps are now cut after its dark albedo is subtracted rather than before, so they measure 16.65 mm3 instead of the 0.81 mm3 sliver the earlier order left.
design_changes.what: Each patch of a marking is clipped to the globe on its own and the lenses fused afterwards, instead of fusing the patches first and intersecting the union with the globe's sphere. The colour bodies are then measured for self-intersection and the marking widened by a graded fraction of a degree and retried until they pass.
design_changes.why: inspect validate measured the earlier build's colour bodies as selfIntersecting on Mercury, Mars and Venus, ten occurrences in all. A marking's outer face is the globe's own sphere, so intersecting a union of overlapping patch tools with that same sphere leaves a neighbouring tool's face running tangent to it along the seam where two patches meet. All sixteen worlds now pass on both armies, and the whole 180-occurrence assembly validates clean.

design_changes.cost: The belt reads as scattered rock rather than as a continuous crumbly mat. The requirement it exists to serve is unaffected and easier to hold: nothing reaches above the field datum, and a seated disc rests on 532.9 mm2 of coplanar contact.
design_changes.what: The belt's rubble is forty-eight disjoint flat-topped boulders of radius 1.60 to 2.60 mm, not a dense mat of a hundred and seventy-six overlapping tapered prisms.
design_changes.why: inspect validate reported invalidTopology on all twelve belt tiles in the assembly package. Measured on the built tile: a face of 0.00034 mm2 and an edge 1.2 micrometres long, made wherever two tapered prisms crossed at a shallow angle, which a taper guarantees because two prisms overlapping at the base grow tangent on the way up. Twelve seeds were tried and every one produced slivers, and both ShapeFix_Shape and ShapeUpgrade_UnifySameDomain left them untouched because they are real geometry rather than a tolerance artefact. Making the rocks disjoint removes the rock-to-rock boolean entirely: worst face 0.00090 mm2, worst edge 0.0125 mm, face count 906 down to 248.

frame_and_floor.focal_point: The near star: the only tall, warm, saturated mass in the frame, a sunflower_yellow plinth standing 2.20 mm proud of a dark_gray field with two orange flames at 18.00 mm rising off the near border. sunflower_yellow appears on no other part of the set.
frame_and_floor.hero_cost: The two flames rise 18.00 mm at the board edge. From the seat opposite that den they stand between the eye and the den cell's far edge. No other component is permitted any of it: the corona tongues are held to 4.00 mm, which is 12.78 mm below the crown of the shortest globe in the set.
frame_and_floor.late_game: Rank reads from three independent channels and ownership from three more, none of which requires picking a piece up. A trapped world sits 3.00 mm below the plane inside a ring of orange or cyan that names whose corona has it; a world in a den sits 2.20 mm above the plane, on the star itself.
frame_and_floor.mid_game: The tightest neighbour pair is two Saturns on adjacent cells: rings Ø30.00 and Ø30.00 across a 72.00 mm span leave 42.00 mm between rim and rim. Disc to disc is 2.13 mm everywhere, which is too tight for fingers, and that is why the grasp point in this set is the globe crown rather than the disc rim: every globe is at least 9.03 mm narrower than the cell pitch and every globe narrows above its equator.
frame_and_floor.ownership_at_thumbnail: Eight white discs read as bright coins on the dark field; eight black discs read as holes in it. Every disc sits inside a cell surrounded by dark_gray board, so no disc is read against the page.
frame_and_floor.second_read: The size ladder along the near back rank: Mercury at Ø13.78 on a3 against Jupiter at Ø26.97 on g3, both on identical Ø34.00 discs, so the disc is a ruler the eye reads the globes against.
frame_and_floor.third_read: Three orange corona wells ring the near star, each recessed 3.00 mm with two 4.00 mm tongues, so the warm mass spreads across four cells instead of one.

limitations.board_reference: The four board panels have no sealed reference image, by the Wish's own decision, and are therefore the only parts not covered by an image-derived comparison. They are carried by the dimensioned spec and were checked by measurement: probed at Z 8 there is air in every terrain pocket, material on every land cell, and material at Z 2 under every pocket floor.
limitations.colour_collision: Earth and Neptune share blue. They are 5.19 mm apart in globe diameter, Earth carries green land and Neptune does not, and they carry different numerals.
limitations.motion: Motion verification is switched off for this run by the immutable run options. Motion is recorded as unverified, never as passed. Nothing in this set moves relative to anything else in any case: there is no assembly, no fastener and no fit beyond a tile dropping into a pocket.
limitations.not_proven: No part of this run demonstrates physical printing, dimensional accuracy on a real bed, material durability, tactile comfort, colour accuracy against real filament, or human play.

measured_data.provenance: Equatorial diameters and axial tilts are observed NASA planetary fact-sheet values carried in the Wish. Every millimetre in the concept is inferred from them by globe_diameter_mm = 13.785 * (D / 4879) ** 0.2.
measured_data.two_jobs: Two real datasets, each doing a job the rules require: the fifth root of the measured diameters is the strength ladder, and the parity inversion of the real obliquities is the ownership cue. Neither is invented.

novelty.claim: An unusual original combination rather than a proven first: a set whose ownership cue is the mirrored real obliquity of eight planets and whose rank ladder is the fifth root of eight measured diameters was not located by a bounded search. Absence from that search is evidence of differentiation, never proof that no similar work exists.
novelty.closest_collisions: Traditional Dou Shou Qi sets carry rank as a printed character or a picture; this set carries no characters at all. Novelty solar-system chess and checkers sets scale planets decoratively, usually uniformly or to fit a mould. Orreries and armillary models carry true orbital relationships but are static display objects.

reference_images.form_taken_from_them: The piece vocabulary: a cylindrical disc with a rounded top edge, a short seat collar, a globe, and a seven-segment numeral read as flush colour rather than relief. The star's two flames, the corona cell's engraved sunburst with two raised corner tongues, the belt tile's rubble ring around a smooth central pad, and the tray's four-by-two sockets all come from them.
reference_images.what_they_are: Twenty sealed images under wish-references: one per unique geometry, sixteen worlds plus the star, a corona cell, a belt tile and a tray. All twenty were opened and are cited as observed sources for form.
reference_images.where_they_were_not_followed: Their globe-to-disc proportions are those of an earlier draft: measured on the images, a globe spans about 0.85 of its disc on every planet except Saturn, where the Wish's own frozen ladder puts Mercury at 0.41 and Jupiter at 0.79. The Wish records that change itself, in its note that Earth's globe moved from 21.08 mm to 16.70 mm after those images were made. The ladder is the invention, so the ladder governs and the whole-piece silhouette-likeness gate was not bound to the superseded proportions; the images were used for form and the ladder for size.

source_game.ladder_note: The Leiden strength ladder is used verbatim, including its ordering at ranks 3 and 4, which differs from some Western listings.
source_game.rights: Traditional Chinese, public domain. No trademarked variant, branded edition, publisher rulebook, artwork or terminology is used, and the set carries no characters at all.
source_game.title: Dou Shou Qi (Jungle Chess, Animal Chess)
source_game.zero_difference_audit: Player count, setup, turn order, legal moves, capture rules, the rat-elephant exception, water and leap rules, trap strength, both victory conditions, and the draw rules are unchanged. Nothing in this set makes an illegal move physically impossible: every cell accepts every piece, the belt carries a flat landing pad, and both dens are identical geometry.
